newsitem.title: USA: Soybeans, wheat prices rise, copper and gasoline up.
newsitem.headline: Soybeans, wheat prices rise, copper and gasoline up.

text.p: Soybean prices rose on Wednesday on rumors of buying interest from China and a cut in Brazil's estimated soybean production by a U.S. government official.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybeans for May delivery closed 2 cents a bushel higher at $8.96 after posting a new life-of-contract high at $9.03-1/2.
Talk circulated early in the day that China was looking to buy U.S. or South American soymeal and soybeans.

"There were a lot of unconfirmed rumors about China," said Roy Huckabay, vice president of LIT, a division of First Options. "My guess is that the rumors about China buying meal probably have some basis in fact but I can't confirm anything has been done."
Also supportive was a report from the U.S. agricultural attache in Brazil that cut Brazil's estimated soybean output this year by 500,000 tonnes to 26.5 million metric tons.

After the close of trading, more bullish news appeared as the U.S. agricultural attache in Argentina cut estimated soybean production to 12.5 million tons, down 750,000 tons from the Agriculture Department's latest estimate on April 11.
Wheat prices also rose as export demand picked up and concerns about freeze damage to the U.S. winter wheat crop resurfaced on reports from crop tours.
Wheat for May delivery closed one cent a bushel higher at $3.95 after rising as high as $4.02 during the session.
Exporters said that Pakistan bought 250,000 tons of U.S. wheat on Wednesday along with 50,000 tons of Australian wheat.

Prices also rose when a crop tour of Oklahoma estimated that state's production this year at only 109 million bushels, down from 121 million estimated last month by an Oklahoma State University survey.

But many crop scouts on a separate Wheat Quality Council tour of Kansas were reporting less damage than initially expected from a hard freeze in the plains in April, and those reports prompted late selling, traders said.

At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, pork belly futures shot up for strong gains after a report showed extremely heavy movement of bellies out of cold storage. Pork bellies for delivery in May ended 2.05 cents a pound up at 89.85 cents.
The exchange reported a net out-movement of 952,000 lbs of bellies last week from warehouses outside Chicago, compared to an in-movement of 333,000 lbs at the same time last year.
"It's a firm market and it's moving higher," said Chuck Levitt, analyst for Alaron Trading Corp.
Copper prices ended higher, buoyed by aluminum prices and strikes in Chile. At the COMEX in New York, copper for July delivery closed up 1.40 cents a pound at 110.45 cents.

The union representing striking workers at Chile's Quebrada Blanca copper mine said it doubted the company's assertion that the facility was still able to produce at half of capacity one week into the strike.
Negotiations at the 75,000-ton per year capacity mine remained were still at a halt.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, gasoline ended higher but gave up much of its early gains as dealers looked askance on oil inventory data which suggested unrealistically strong demand amid tightening gasoline supply.
Gasoline for June delivery ended up 0.61 cent at 60.92 cents a gallon after rising to session high of 61.65 cents.
The American Petroleum Institute said gasoline stocks fell 3.6 million barrels for the week ended May 2, while dealers had been expecting a rise of up to two million barrels.

"We thought demand was overstated and supply was understated. I think it may have something to do with the change to summer (gasoline specifications), so the data may normalize after this," said Michael Busby, trader with Northville Industries in Melville, New York.
June crude oil closed four cents a barrel lower at $19.62 while June heating oil ended 0.45 cent a gallon lower at 53.08 cents.
